rule: Every number on screen or in VO must be listed here with a source URL. `display` is the exact on-screen string. `confidence`: verified = read in the primary source this session; secondary = reputable secondary source read this session; anecdote = widely reported story, label it on screen.

facts.claim: Basaltic lava (the common Hawaiian kind) erupts at roughly 1,000–1,250 °C; Hawaiian basalt is usually around 1,100 °C. Kīlauea Iki 1959 measurements: 1,060–1,190 °C.
facts.sourceTitle: Oregon State University, Volcano World — 'How hot is lava?' (table: Basalt 1000–1250 °C; 'Hawaiian lava (basalt) is usually around 1100 C.')
facts.quote: Hawaiian lava (basalt) is usually around 1100 C.
facts.secondaryTitle: Ault, Eaton & Richter (1961), USGS — 'Temperatures of the erupting basalt ranged between 1060° and 1190°C.'
facts.note: VO says 'around 1,100 degrees Celsius'. Rhyolite is cooler (700–900 °C) — the reel is about a basaltic volcano; do not generalise to all volcanoes.

facts.claim: Molten basaltic lava is about 3,100 kg/m³, roughly three times the density of a human body (≈ 1,000 kg/m³, close to water), so a person would not sink into it.
facts.sourceTitle: Eric James Beyer, 'What If You Fell Into Lava?', Sciencing (Feb 10, 2025) — 'Lava … has a density of roughly 3,100 kilograms per cubic meter, making it three times denser' than a human body of 'around 1,000 kilograms per cubic meter'.
facts.quote: Lava, on the other hand, has a density of roughly 3,100 kilograms per cubic meter, making it three times denser.
facts.secondaryTitle: Wikipedia, 'Basalt' — average density of solid basalt 2.9 g/cm³ (2,900 kg/m³); the melt is a little less dense. Either way the ratio to a human body rounds to 3×.
facts.note: Human-body density ≈ 1,000 kg/m³ is textbook general knowledge (945–1,020 kg/m³ between full inhale and exhale); no primary study cited. Some volcanologists argue a body could slowly sink in very fluid lava; the reel says 'you float' as the first-order physics, which every source agrees on.

facts.claim: Basaltic lava has a viscosity of about 10²–10³ Pa·s; water is about 10⁻³ Pa·s — lava is on the order of 100,000 to 1,000,000 times more viscous than water.
facts.sourceTitle: Simon Fraser University, EASC 421 'Effusive volcanism' lecture notes — 'basalt = 10² – 10³ Pa·s, water = 10⁻³ Pa·s, olive oil = 10⁻¹ Pa·s'.
facts.secondaryTitle: Sciencing (2025): 'Lava is also around 100,000 times more viscous than water'.
facts.onScreenSource: Basalt 10²–10³ Pa·s · water 10⁻³ · SFU Earth Sci.
facts.note: 100,000× is the LOW end of the range (10² / 10⁻³); the high end is 1,000,000×. The VO says 'a hundred thousand times' — conservative on purpose. Pāhoehoe field measurements (380–6,000 Pa·s) sit inside this range.

notUsed.claim: Some discussions argue a person might initially float, then sink as body water flashes to steam, or that low-viscosity alkaline basalts (Erta Ale) could let a body sink slowly.
